sentences.text: Dilophosaurus was the largest-known land animal in North America during the Early Jurassic, reaching approximately 7 meters in length and weighing about 400 kilograms.
This predator possessed a slender, lightly built body and a proportionally large skull equipped with long, curved, thin, and sideways-compressed teeth.
Three skeletons were discovered in northern Arizona in 1940, with the two best-preserved specimens collected in 1942.

Samuel P. Welles initially named the most complete specimen *Megalosaurus wetherilli* in 1954, discovered a larger skeleton in 1964, and reclassified the species into the new genus *Dilophosaurus* in 1970 due to the presence of skull crests.
Dilophosaurus was likely an active, bipedal predator that may have hunted large animals, as well as smaller animals and fish.
The function of Dilophosaurus crests is unknown, but they were likely used for visual displays like species recognition or sexual selection rather than combat.
Dilophosaurus may have grown rapidly, gaining 30 to 35 kilograms per year in its early life.
Dilophosaurus was designated the state dinosaur of Connecticut based on fossil tracks found there.
Dilophosaurus belongs to the superfamily Coelophysoidea and is considered a member of the family Dilophosauridae, though this classification is debated by some researchers.
Marsh and Rowe concluded in 2020 that all known Dilophosaurus specimens belong to a single taxon, with differences attributed to maturity and preservation.
In 1998, Lamanna and colleagues determined that *D. sinensis* is identical to *Sinosaurus triassicus*, leading to its reclassification.
Dilophosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically from the Sinemurian to Toarcian stages, approximately 186 million years ago in what is now North America.
Paleontologists debated whether Dilophosaurus was a basal genus that gave rise to ceratosaurians and tetanurans, or if it was simply a large coelophysid.
This skull structure led to the early hypothesis that Dilophosaurus was a scavenger, with front teeth too weak to kill and hold large prey.
In 2017, Wang and colleagues suggested that the species formerly known as *D. sinensis* might be a separate species, *S. sinensis*, despite agreeing it belongs in the genus *Sinosaurus*.

Some researchers interpret trackway impressions of a Dilophosaurus-like theropod as showing feather impressions around the belly and feet, while others interpret them as sedimentary artifacts, though this does not rule out the presence of feathers.
